**LinkedIn — the text-to-SQL agent whose real product turned out to be the repair loop (2024)**

On 9 December 2024 LinkedIn's engineering team published a detailed account of SQL Bot, the text-to-SQL assistant embedded in its DARWIN data platform, described as a multi-agent system "built on top of LangChain and LangGraph". The interesting engineering is not the generation step. It is where the team chose to spend state.

Context narrowing is done in stages, and every stage is a recall bet paid to keep the prompt affordable. Access-popularity filtering cuts millions of tables to a few thousand; personalisation using org charts narrows further; embedding-based retrieval returns the top 20 tables, and, in their words, "we employ a LLM re-ranker to select the top 7 tables for query writing". A second re-ranker then picks fields. Behind it sits a knowledge graph of schemas, field classifications, join patterns and certified example queries.

The cycle is the part that a chain cannot express. Rather than one-shot generation, SQL Bot plans and solves incrementally, and a separate self-correction agent — equipped with tools to retrieve additional tables or fields — repairs validation errors. Note what that means for state design: the repair node can widen its own context, so the loop's exit condition is a validator's verdict, not the model's confidence. The human-triggered version of the same path, "Fix with AI", was "easy to develop but has very high usage—accounting for 80% of our sessions".

Their measurement honesty is worth as much as the architecture. The benchmark runs to over 130 questions across 10 product areas, and once they admitted multiple valid answers per question they found that "without these additional answers, we underreported recall by 10-15%". A survey put ~95% of users at "Passes" or above on query accuracy but only ~40% at "Very Good" or "Excellent" — the gap between acceptable and good is precisely the territory the repair loop occupies. Embedding the bot in DARWIN rather than shipping it standalone increased adoption 5–10x.

When you lay out your own StateGraph, the decisions that carry the most weight are which node owns the validator, what the self-correction node is permitted to add to state, and where you checkpoint so a human can take the wheel mid-graph. Design the repair path as the busiest edge in the graph rather than the exception, and size your channel reducers for a state that grows on every retry.

**MetaGPT — roles bought structure, and the verification loop bought correctness (2023–2024)**

MetaGPT (Hong et al., published 2023, ICLR 2024) is the research ancestor of the role model CrewAI later made popular: a Product Manager, Architect, Project Manager, Engineer and QA agent, each carrying a role prompt. Its thesis is that standard operating procedures should be encoded into the prompt sequence, and that agents should hand off structured artefacts — a PRD, a design document naming the Python package and file structure, a task list — rather than free-form conversation.

Measured against ChatDev on the paper's SoftwareDev tasks, the structured-handoff design wins on the metrics that matter for delivery: executability 3.75 against 2.25 on a 1–4 scale, 124.3 tokens to generate one line of code against 248.9, and a human revision cost of 0.83 against 2.5. Read the token line carefully. MetaGPT consumed more tokens in absolute terms (31,255 against 19,292); the gain is per unit of delivered code, not per run. Structured handoff costs tokens up front and repays them in work you do not have to redo.

The ablation is the part worth memorising. Adding executable feedback — the Engineer actually running and debugging its own output — improved Pass@1 by 4.2% on HumanEval and 5.4% on MBPP, and dropped the human revision cost from 2.25 to 0.83, on the way to the reported 85.9% and 87.7% Pass@1 headline figures. Roles and document schemas alone did not produce that. Role definition bought structure; the verification loop bought correctness. They are separate purchases.

That separation maps onto the CrewAI decisions in front of you. A backstory plus a tightly specified `expected_output` is your SOP encoding, and it constrains the shape of the handoff — which is much of why sequential crews behave more predictably than hierarchical ones, where an LLM manager reallocates work opaquely. But `context=[research_task]` injects a prior task's entire output as text. Nothing in that chain asks whether the prior output was right.

So before adding a fifth specialist to a crew, establish whether any agent actually executes or checks the previous one's work, or merely reads it and writes prose about it. An editor agent that fact-checks against a tool is a verification step; an editor agent that reviews from the transcript is another opinion. If no step in your crew can fail objectively, you have bought an org chart rather than accuracy, and the token bill will scale with the headcount.

**MAST — the failures were conversational, not cognitive (2025)**

In March 2025 a UC Berkeley-led team (Cemri, Pan, Yang and colleagues, with Zaharia, Gonzalez and Stoica among the authors) published the first empirically grounded taxonomy of multi-agent LLM failure. Six expert annotators worked through over 200 execution traces drawn from seven systems — AG2, the AutoGen lineage, alongside Magentic-One, ChatDev, MetaGPT, HyperAgent, AppWorld and OpenManus. Three annotators independently labelled a shared subset and reached Cohen's Kappa of 0.88 after three rounds of refinement, and the resulting MAST-Data release runs to over 1,600 annotated traces.

The taxonomy has 14 failure modes in three categories, and the distribution is the finding: specification issues 41.77%, inter-agent misalignment 36.94%, task verification 21.30%. The six misalignment modes read like an inventory of things a GroupChat does — conversation reset, failure to ask for clarification, task derailment, information withholding, ignoring another agent's input, and reasoning-action mismatch. Two of the specification modes, loss of conversation history and being unaware of termination conditions, are literally the `max_round` and `is_termination_msg` settings you configure and then never revisit.

The baseline shows the scale of it. ChatDev, one of the better-known open-source systems, achieved only 33.33% correctness on the authors' ProgramDev benchmark. These were not model-capability failures. They were conversation-management failures, produced by agents that were individually competent.

Then the uncomfortable result. The authors tried the obvious repairs: sharpening the agent role specifications yielded +9.4% in success rate, and adding a verification step targeting high-level task objectives on top of existing code-level checks yielded a further +15.6% absolute on ProgramDev. Their own reading is that these gains remain insufficient for reliable behaviour and that the failures "require more fundamental changes in system design". Prompt-level repair moved the number without fixing the class of bug.

The practical consequence for the code in this lesson: `speaker_selection_method="auto"` hands routing to a model that carries no view of termination state and no memory of which agent has already been ignored. Instrument for the named modes — log resets, derailment and silent withholding as first-class events — and replace auto selection with a custom function and explicit termination once a chat exceeds three participants. Ask first, though, whether the task needs a conversation at all: specification and misalignment together account for close to 79% of the failures catalogued here, and both categories only exist because the work was split across agents.

**Airbnb — the orchestration they wrote instead of the framework they could have adopted (2025)**

Airbnb carried nearly 3.5K React component test files written against Enzyme, a library built for an older React and reliant on deep access to component internals. Migrating them by hand to React Testing Library was estimated at 1.5 years of engineering time. The team finished in six weeks using a pipeline they built themselves, and the write-up is unusually specific about the machinery.

Read the design against the five primitives. The state container is per-file, not per-conversation. The execution loop is a state machine whose steps are an Enzyme refactor, fixing Jest, fixing lint and tsc, then marking the file complete — and the validator at each step is the actual toolchain, not an LLM judge. Steps retry "multiple times until they passed or we reached a limit". Because each file's state is independent and each verdict is objective, the whole corpus runs concurrently and failures are isolated rather than poisoning a shared message history. There is no orchestration layer in the multi-agent sense at all, which is the point.

The numbers explain why a general framework would have bought them little. They "successfully migrated 75% of our target files in just four hours". The long tail then took four days of prompt and script refinement under a "sample, tune, and sweep" strategy to reach 97% of the 3.5K files, with the remaining 3% done by hand over another week. Most files passed within about 10 attempts; the stubborn ones were retried anywhere between 50 and 100 times. Prompts grew to "anywhere between 40,000 to 100,000 tokens, pulling in as many as 50 related files" — sibling tests, RTL examples, imports, component source.

The cost is where the honesty sits. Brute-force retry against a 100,000-token dynamic context is expensive per file and would be indefensible if the verdict were fuzzy; Airbnb could afford it because the verdict was a test run and a type check. They state that the total, including API usage and six weeks of engineering, still beat the manual estimate, but they publish no dollar figure — so treat the economics as directionally reported, not as a benchmark you can quote.

That gives you the entry test for building your own. Airbnb had two preconditions: an objective per-step validator, and enough repetitions of the same task to amortise the tuning. With both, the five primitives are a few hundred lines and you keep full control of retry policy, context assembly and concurrency — control no framework will hand you. Without an objective validator, your loop has no honest exit condition, and you are better served adopting a framework whose checkpointing and human-in-the-loop machinery someone else already hardened.

**Octomind — twelve months on LangChain, then out (2023–2024)**

Octomind runs AI agents that generate and repair end-to-end Playwright tests. They adopted LangChain in early 2023, ran it in production for over twelve months, and removed it during 2024, publishing the reasoning in a post that reached the front page of Hacker News on 20 June 2024. It is the rare migration write-up that names the mechanism rather than the mood.

What forced it was the direction of their requirements, not a defect. The framework's promise — idea to working code in an afternoon — held while their needs stayed close to the shapes it modelled. As those needs became more sophisticated it inverted into friction. Their specific complaint is structural: abstractions layered on other abstractions, so understanding an API correctly meant holding nested indirection in your head, and time that should have gone into features went into large stack traces and debugging framework internals they had not written.

The second argument generalises beyond one library. When behaviour needed changing below the abstraction line, the seam had been abstracted away — the thing you need to reach is exactly the thing a high-level framework hides. And in a field whose core concepts turn over on a monthly cadence, an abstraction designed to be durable is a bet against your own roadmap. Their illustration was deliberately unflattering to both sides: for a trivial task the framework saved nothing over the provider SDK, and for a hard one it charged indirection.

What they replaced it with was modular building blocks rather than a rival framework, and they report a simplified codebase and a more productive team. Two things keep this honest. First, removing a framework does not remove the work it was doing — retries, streaming, tracing, provider adapters and tool-schema plumbing all become yours to maintain, and that bill arrives later than the celebration. Second, in the same discussion LangChain's chief executive Harrison Chase conceded the substance of the critique: "The initial version of LangChain was pretty high level and absolutely abstracted away too much." A framework author saying that in public is stronger evidence than any comparison table.

So when you score the lock-in dimension, stop counting how much framework code you would have to delete. Count seams. Write down, before you commit, the three lowest-level behaviours you expect to override — retry and backoff policy, exact message construction, tool-result formatting are the usual three — and verify you can reach each without forking the dependency or monkey-patching internals. If you cannot reach them, the migration is already on your roadmap; you have not yet been told the date.
